title: Heap, stacks, and static allocation

spans.text: Goal: apply “Heap, stacks, and static allocation” to a real program or device. The key principle is: Release allocated memory and plan long-lived objects deliberately. In a project, follow this guidance: Check task-creation results and stack use; budget RAM across tasks, queues, and buffers.
QUESTION: What will this example do? Predict the result first.
Prints allocation success when the FreeRTOS heap has at least 128 bytes available.

Every FreeRTOS task consumes its own stack; tasks, queues, and timers may also allocate from the kernel heap. Creation can fail when memory is exhausted, while stack overflow can corrupt state. Measure stack high-water marks and minimum heap, and consider static allocation where supported; do not copy demo sizes into production without measurement.

Key line: `void setup() { Serial.begin(115200); void* memory = pvPortMalloc(128); if (memory != nullptr) { Serial.println("128 bytes available"); vPortFree(memory); } else { Serial.println("heap exhausted"); } }`
What it does: Release allocated memory and plan long-lived objects deliberately.
Why it is used: Check task-creation results and stack use; budget RAM across tasks, queues, and buffers.
If omitted or changed: Stack-size units vary by port/API; the ESP32 Arduino Core API shown here uses bytes.
